teaser.text: Diploma sells specialist products and practical support to customers in healthcare, industry and infrastructure. Its financial story is the movement of money through those specialist businesses: customers pay for dependable solutions, while Diploma pays for products, people, stock and growth.

blocks.heading: What has to go right for Diploma, and what could go wrong?

paragraphs.text: The bear case assumes FY26 delivers, but 15% organic growth then proves unsustainable. Aerospace and industrial demand weaken, Controls and Seals slow, and Life Sciences cannot fully offset them. Inventory absorbs cash, write-downs rise and doubts about acquisitions compress the multiple.

The base case becomes more credible if organic growth settles toward the 5% medium-term model and margins move toward 20%. The bull case requires growth to remain above that model, strong margins to persist and acquired businesses to earn attractive returns.

blocks.heading: How much cash does Diploma really make?

paragraphs.text: Profit is not the same as cash. Inventory bought before sale reduces cash first, which is why working capital absorbed £58.9 million in H1 2026. Diploma still produced £110.7 million of free cash flow after operating needs, tax, interest and capital spending. Net debt to EBITDA was 0.8x at 31 March 2026, but EBITDA is not cash and later acquisitions changed the picture. The valuation therefore begins with strong growth, but it must be tested against cash and acquisition returns.
Recent share dilution was modest, but the share count still matters because acquisitions funded with shares can reduce each existing shareholder’s claim on future earnings.

blocks.heading: Is Diploma's dividend covered by its cash?

paragraphs.text: Free cash flow conversion measures how much adjusted earnings becomes free cash flow after operating cash flow and capital expenditure, but before acquisitions, disposals, borrowing transactions and dividends. Diploma’s model assumes 90% conversion. FY2025 reached 105%, while the six months to March 2026 reached 76%.

paragraphs.text: The first test is the FY26 outcome and the final dividend announcement scheduled for 17 November 2026. Delivery of upgraded growth and margin guidance would support the base or bull path.

During FY27–FY29, inventory, receivables and cash conversion will decide whether earnings become debt reduction and acquisition capacity. Continued working-capital absorption would move the forecast toward the bear case.

blocks.heading: What is Diploma's dividend yield today?

paragraphs.text: Adjusted earnings rose from £106.1m in FY2021 to £236.0m in FY2025. Net income was £184.9m in FY2025. Cash conversion fell to 76% in H1 2026 after £58.9m of working-capital absorption. Forward P/E was 29.5x and price to book was 10.1x. Dividend yield was 0.8% and buyback yield was 0.0%.

earnings.opening: Diploma's next results are due November 17, 2026. Diploma's cash conversion is the one thing to watch.
earnings.closing: The full memo also explains Diploma's business, rivals, management and risks.

blocks.heading: What has Diploma guided for FY2026?

paragraphs.text: Management has moved from expecting a good year to demanding an exceptional one. At November 2025 results, Diploma expected 6% organic growth for FY2026. By May, it expected 12%. In July, the target reached 14.0% organic growth and a 26.5% operating margin for FY2026. Acquisitions were expected to add 6.0% to reported growth, implying operating profit growth of about 42.0%.

Diploma’s medium-term model is more measured. It assumes slower organic and total revenue growth, a 20.0% adjusted margin, prudent leverage and a progressive dividend. It is a guide to a sustainable business, not a promise that the exceptional FY2026 pace will continue.

blocks.heading: What has Diploma said about promises kept?

paragraphs.text: There is encouraging evidence: Diploma said its FY2025 results were ahead of expectations, and the July update described another upgrade. But those examples do not establish a complete record of beating forecasts. The next result must show both that trading held through the year-end and that acquired businesses contributed as planned.

blocks.heading: What has Diploma's revenue and profit done in the last eight reported periods?

paragraphs.text: For the six months to March 2026, revenue and the company’s earnings measure grew faster than net income. Diluted EPS rose only modestly. This means the businesses performed strongly, but acquisition amortisation, financing effects and other adjustments continued to absorb part of the improvement before it reached shareholders.

blocks.heading: What should readers watch in Diploma's next results?

paragraphs.text: The full-year results due on 17 November 2026 will show whether Diploma converted its upgraded outlook into both profit and cash. A strong result must be more than a high operating margin: it must explain where growth came from and what it required financially.
